Configuration reference

Configuration is at the foot of the shelf. Its pages are in two groups: Basic, the ones most people change, and Advanced, the rest. About is on its own below them.

Basic

  • Appearance — theme, text, the list, the article, and the layout.
  • Language and region — the interface language, and how dates and times are written.
  • Navigation — when an opened article counts as read, swipe gestures, and whether the shelf is a sidebar or hidden.
  • Keyboard — the shortcut list.
  • Share — what a share sends.
  • Notifications — announcements and notices.
  • Sources — everything you follow, with the filter, the tick boxes and the bulk actions described under Managing sources, and the order the list is kept in.
  • Fetching — how often to check, on which connections and on battery, and how many sources at once.
  • Summaries — whether summaries are written, where, how many at a time and per check, the summary language, and suggested tags.
  • Background work — what the status strip shows while the app works, and, on a phone, Configuration › Basic › Background work › With the screen off › Keep working with the screen off, which keeps checks, summaries, model downloads and sync running after the screen goes off.
  • Tags — the vocabulary: every tag, to rename, merge or remove.

Configuration › Basic › Navigation › Mark as read is worth knowing about: Never means only you mark things read, Immediately means opening counts, After a few seconds means passing through does not, and When you reach the end waits for the bottom of the article.

Advanced

  • On-device model — models on this device and finding new ones, and the processor a model runs on.
  • LLM server — the address, model and key of a server that summarizes.
  • Sync — sync on or off, the server address, when it runs on its own, whether this device keeps everything, another device, the recovery code, and deleting the copy on the server.
  • Accounts — the sites this device is signed in to, where the build supports signing in.
  • Tokens and API & MCP — in Premium only, because all three doors are: a free build has no tab and no ports rather than switches that refuse.
  • Your data — export, import, backup and restore, duplicate sources, how long article text and pictures are kept, and the system backup.
  • Statistics — what summarizing has used, and what the library holds.
  • Debug — the trace: everything that ran and everything that failed, which is the first place to look when something did not happen.
  • Development — Missing details, which re-fetches metadata, a model comparison, experiments, and Erase everything.

API & MCP

Three doors, each with its own port, its own choice of which addresses it answers on, its own token and its own switch: the REST API a browser extension or another program puts something in through, Metrics for a monitoring system, and MCP, which a model answers on. They start on 8765, 8766 and 8767, and none of them needs another to be open.

Use TLS (HTTPS), under the three doors, is off by default and switches all three to HTTPS at once. The first time, the app makes a certificate for this device, naming its host name and its addresses, and keeps the key with the other secrets. Clients must then use https:// and trust that certificate: the page shows its SHA-256 fingerprint, with a button to copy it, so a client can pin it. New certificate makes another one, and every client that pinned the old fingerprint must be given the new one. The MCP command-line wrapper picks the certificate up by itself; restart its client after a new certificate.

The terminal reader is not one of these. It opens the library file directly, needs no door open and no port, and is free.

Your data

Export and Import, a section each: OPML for sources, and your library in full. Backup and restore copies the whole library to one file and back; Configuration › Advanced › Your data › Backup and restore › Include sign-ins and tokens, off each time, adds every account's sign-in and every token to it, encrypted with a passphrase you type twice. That file and its passphrase together sign in to those accounts. A restore asks for the passphrase; a wrong or forgotten one still restores the library, and leaves this device's sign-ins as they were. Also Configuration › Advanced › Your data › Duplicate sources, which looks for the same channel followed under two addresses and offers to merge the pairs it finds.

About

Version, the open-source licences, the privacy policy, the end-user licence and the terms. On Linux, Check for updates. The privacy policy, the licence and the terms open inside the app, from the copy the app was built with, so they work offline. Open on the site on that page shows the newest version in your browser (Configuration › Basic › About › About › Privacy policy, and the same for the other two).
